intro: An observational study records data without imposing a treatment, so it can show association but usually cannot establish cause because of confounding (a variable linked to both the explanatory variable and the response). An experiment deliberately assigns treatments, and with random assignment it can support cause-and-effect conclusions. Only a well-designed experiment with random assignment allows a causal claim.

items.prompt: Researchers compare health of people who chose to exercise vs those who did not. Study type and limitation?

steps: No treatment was imposed; behavior was only observed.
So it is an observational study.
Confounding (for example, diet) means it cannot prove exercise causes better health.
solution.answer: Observational study; confounding prevents a causal claim.

items.prompt: Subjects are randomly assigned to a new drug or a placebo, then outcomes are compared. Study type?

steps: Treatments (drug vs placebo) were deliberately assigned.
So it is a (randomized) experiment, which can support causation.

items.prompt: In a study linking coffee to longer life, name a possible confounder.

steps: A confounder is linked to both coffee drinking and lifespan.
For instance, coffee drinkers might exercise more or smoke less.
Such a variable confounds the coffee-lifespan relationship.
solution.answer: A lifestyle factor like exercise or smoking.
